blocks.text: Every request an MCP client sends is a small act of faith, it goes out over the wire and the client simply waits, trusting that something will come back. The response message is that something.
" Understanding the shape of a response, and how it ties itself back to the request that caused it, is the other half of the request and response pattern that JSON-RPC is built around.
1. What a Response Message Is

A response message is what a server sends back for every request it receives, and only for requests, notifications never get one. It is a JSON object with three required parts, the jsonrpc version string, an id that copies the id from the request it answers, and either a result or an error, never both and never neither.

Because a response is defined entirely by what it contains rather than by any special wrapper or envelope, a client can recognize one the instant it sees a message with an id and either a result or an error field, no method field is present, which is one of the clearest structural signals that distinguish a response from a request.

code.content: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "result": { "tools": [ { "name": "get_weather", "description": "Look up current weather for a city" } ] } }

blocks.text: The jsonrpc field itself is always the literal string "2.0", it never changes between requests, responses, or notifications, it simply confirms which flavor of the underlying wire protocol every message on this connection is speaking.
2. Matching Responses to Requests via id

The single most important job a response performs is telling the client which request it belongs to. The client generated an id when it sent the request, kept that id in a small table of pending calls, and now checks every incoming response's id against that table to find the right match.

This matters enormously once a client has several requests in flight at once. A client might ask for a tool list, a resource read, and a prompt fetch within the same second, and the responses could come back in any order, the id is the only reliable way to know which answer belongs to which question.

This is why a client should never reuse an id while a previous request using that same id is still pending, doing so would make a returning response ambiguous, there would be no way to tell which of the two requests it was actually answering.
3. The result Field for a Successful Response

blocks.alt: A successful response carries a result field

blocks.text: When a request succeeds, the response carries a result field, and result is deliberately open, its shape is entirely determined by which method the original request called. There is no single universal result schema, tools/call returns something different from resources/read, which returns something different again from initialize.

This is a normal and intentional part of JSON-RPC, the protocol itself only guarantees that result will be present on success, and it hands off the responsibility of defining what is actually inside result to whatever method-specific contract MCP defines for that particular method.

blocks.title: result can be any valid JSON value
blocks.content: While most MCP methods return an object, the JSON-RPC specification itself only requires result to be a valid JSON value, an object, array, string, number, or even a boolean, MCP simply chooses to define object shaped results for its own methods.

blocks.text: Even though the exact shape of result varies by method, the client always knows which method it called for a given id, since it stored that alongside the pending request, so it always knows how to interpret the result once it arrives.
4. Response Shape for tools/call

A tools/call response wraps its answer in a content array, a list of pieces of output, most commonly text blocks, but potentially images or embedded resources too. There is also an optional isError flag that lets a tool report its own failure without that failure ever becoming a protocol level error.

code.content: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 12, "result": { "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "It is 21 degrees and cloudy in Lisbon" } ], "isError": false } }

blocks.text: Notice that isError lives inside result rather than being a protocol level error, that placement is deliberate, a tool that fails is still a successful protocol exchange, the server did what was asked and reported back, it just happens to be reporting that the underlying operation did not succeed.
5. Response Shape for resources/read

A resources/read response returns a contents array, since a single URI can, in principle, expand into more than one piece of content. Each entry names the uri it came from and carries either text or a base64 encoded blob, along with a mimeType describing what it is.

A single resources/read call returning more than one entry in contents is uncommon but valid, this can happen for a resource that expands into several logical pieces, a directory style resource being one example.
6. Response Shape for prompts/get

A prompts/get response returns a messages array, a ready to use sequence of role and content pairs that the client can hand straight to a language model. It may also include a description explaining what the prompt is for, filled in with whatever arguments the caller supplied.

code.content: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 14, "result": { "description": "Summarize a support ticket", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": { "type": "text", "text": "Summarize this ticket in two sentences" } } ] } }

blocks.text: The messages array in a prompts/get response is intentionally shaped the same way most chat completion APIs expect their input, which is precisely what makes it directly usable without the client needing to translate between two different message formats.
7. Response Shape for initialize

The response to initialize is the one place where a single result carries the most structure of any method in MCP, it returns the protocolVersion the server has settled on, the server's capabilities, and a serverInfo object naming and versioning the server itself, all three arriving together in the one response that completes the handshake.

Everything the client learns about the server, its name, its version, the protocol version it is willing to speak, and what it supports, arrives packed into this one response, which is why initialize is sometimes called the single most information dense exchange in the whole session.
8. Responses With Empty or Minimal Results

Not every successful call has anything interesting to report back. The ping method, used purely to check that a connection is alive, returns a result that is simply an empty object, there is nothing to say beyond the fact that the response happened at all.

An empty result is not a special case that needs different handling from a client, it is still a perfectly ordinary success, still matched by id, still distinguishable from an error purely by the presence of the result key rather than an error key.

A client should still wait for this response before considering the ping complete, an empty object is not the same as no response at all, the distinction between a slow but healthy connection and a genuinely dead one depends entirely on whether this small response eventually shows up.
9. A Response Never Has Both result and error

blocks.alt: result and error never both appear

blocks.text: The JSON-RPC specification treats result and error as mutually exclusive, a well formed response contains exactly one of them, never both, and never neither. A message that somehow had both would be malformed, and a client encountering one should treat it as a protocol violation rather than try to interpret it as a partial success.

blocks.title: Presence, not content, decides success or failure
blocks.content: A client should branch on which key is present rather than inspecting the value inside result, checking "result" in message is the correct and simplest test for success.

code.content:
// malformed, never produced by a correct server
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "result": { "ok": true }, "error": { "code": -32603, "message": "Internal error" } }

blocks.text: 10. Exactly One Response Per Request

blocks.alt: One request gets exactly one response

blocks.text: Every request gets exactly one response, never zero and never more than one. A server that wants to report progress while working on a long running request does that through separate notification messages sent alongside the work, the request itself still resolves with a single, final response once the work is done.

This one to one relationship is what makes the pending request table on the client side reliable, once a response with a given id has been received and handled, the client can retire that id, confident no second response for it is still coming.

If a server were to somehow send two responses for the same id, a well behaved client treats the first one as authoritative and discards the second as unexpected, since the protocol never promises to define behavior for that case.
11. Responses May Arrive Out of Order

blocks.alt: Response A with id 2 can arrive before response B with id 1

blocks.text: Nothing in the protocol requires responses to come back in the same order their requests were sent. A slow resources/read issued first can easily be overtaken by a fast tools/call issued a moment later, and the client has to be built to expect that.

This is one of the reasons a client should never rely on send order to guess which response belongs to which call, doing so happens to work while everything is fast and uncontended, and then breaks in production the first time one request is slower than the one after it.
12. Nested Data Inside result

Because result is just a JSON object, it is free to nest arrays, objects, and further structure as deeply as the method needs. tools/list returns an array of tool definitions, each one itself a small object with a name, description, and an inputSchema that is itself a full JSON schema document.

A client parsing a response should not assume a flat shape, it needs to know, method by method, how deep the structure goes and what each nested piece means, which is exactly why MCP defines a specific result shape for every method rather than leaving it to guesswork.

Clients that use a typed language often define a dedicated response type per method, matching the nested shape field for field, so that a malformed or unexpected result surfaces as a clear parsing error rather than a confusing runtime failure somewhere deep in application code.
13. How a Client Correlates a Response

blocks.alt: A response is checked against a pending requests map to find the matched request

blocks.text: In practice, a client keeps a map from pending id to whatever callback or promise is waiting on that request. When a response arrives, the client looks up its id in that map, resolves the corresponding promise with the result, or rejects it with the error, and removes the entry.

A production grade version of this pattern usually adds a timeout as well, if no response for a given id arrives within a reasonable window, the pending entry is rejected with a timeout error and removed, rather than sitting forever waiting for a reply that may never come.

The same pending table pattern works regardless of transport, whether messages travel over standard input and output or over an HTTP based transport, the client side bookkeeping of id to pending callback stays exactly the same.
14. Responses Compared to Notifications

A response and a notification can look deceptively similar, both can carry a params like payload of data, but a response always has an id copied from a real request and always contains result or error, while a notification never has an id at all and is not a reply to anything specific.

If a client ever finds itself trying to match an incoming message's id against its pending table and finds no id field present, that is the signal it is looking at a notification, not a response, and the message should be routed to notification handling instead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Message type","Has id","Has method","Has result or error"],"rows":[["Request","yes","yes","no"],["Response","yes, copied","no","yes, exactly one"],["Notification","no","yes","no"]]}

blocks.text: 15. Responses Compared to Requests Structurally

A request and a response are, in a sense, mirror images. A request has a method and params describing what to do, a response has a result or error describing what happened, and the id is the one field both share, planted by the request and echoed back unchanged by the response.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Present in request","Present in response"],"rows":[["jsonrpc","yes","yes"],["id","yes","yes, copied from the request"],["method","yes","no"],["params","optional","no"],["result or error","no","exactly one is required"]]}

blocks.text: 16. Why Responses Are Deliberately Minimal

A response never repeats the method name, never repeats the params that produced it, it only carries the id and the outcome. This minimalism keeps responses small and keeps the burden of remembering what was asked squarely on the side that asked it, the client, which already has that information sitting in its own pending table.

That design choice also means a response is meaningless in isolation, a bare { "id": 7, "result": {} } tells you nothing about what happened without also knowing, from the client's own records, what request id 7 actually was.

This is also why logging a response on its own is rarely useful for debugging, a well built client logs the request and its response together, keyed by id, so the full story, what was asked and what came back, is visible in one place.
Worked Example
A client calls tools/call to run a search_docs tool, then trace the response all the way back to the caller.

items: 1. Client generates id 55 and sends { jsonrpc: "2.0", id: 55, method: "tools/call", params: { name: "search_docs", arguments: { query: "refund policy" } } }.
2. Client stores a pending future keyed by 55 and returns it to the calling code.
3. Server runs the tool and builds a result, a content array with one text block summarizing what it found.
4. Server sends back { jsonrpc: "2.0", id: 55, result: { content: [ { type: "text", text: "Refunds are accepted within 30 days" } ] } }.
5. Client receives the message, sees id 55 with a result field, looks up 55 in its pending table, and resolves that future with the result.
6. The calling code, which had been awaiting that future, now receives the content array and renders it to the user.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes

items: Assuming responses arrive in the same order requests were sent, instead of matching strictly by id.
Checking the contents of result to decide success or failure instead of checking whether the result key is present at all.
Forgetting that a tools/call response can carry isError true inside a normal result, and treating every tool failure as a protocol level error.
Leaking pending table entries by never cleaning them up after a response, or a timeout, has already been handled.
Assuming every method returns the same result shape, rather than looking up the specific shape defined for that method.
Trying to parse a notification as if it were a response because it happens to carry a params object.

blocks.text: Practice

Write a small response handler that takes an incoming JSON-RPC message and a pending requests map, and correctly resolves or rejects the right entry, ignoring the message entirely if it turns out to be a notification.
Key Takeaway

A response message is defined by three things, an id copied from its request, and exactly one of result or error, with the shape of result itself determined entirely by which method was called. Matching by id, not by order of arrival, is what lets a client juggle many requests in flight at once.
The next topic, Notifications, looks at the other kind of message JSON-RPC sends, ones with no id at all and no response expected, and why that structural difference exists in the first place.
